title: Ministers pledge legal reforms ahead of Nepal infrastructure summit - The Kathmandu Post
description: Ministers pledge legal reforms ahead of Nepal infrastructure summit  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Three ministers have expressed a common commitment to reform existing laws to create a more conducive environment for investment and development and to spur economic activity.

Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sobita Gautam, Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal and Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle appeared on the same platform at a workshop on “Legal Reforms for Investment and Development” organised by the Ministry of Infrastructure Development on Friday as part of preparations for the Nepal Infrastructure Conference 2026.

They agreed on the need to make laws more development- and business-friendly to accelerate economic activity. Finance Minister Wagle said the government was amending laws based on suggestions from the private sector.

“We are introducing 27 new laws in the current fiscal year as part of economic reforms,” Wagle said. “Since becoming finance minister, I have initiated the process of repealing old Acts and drafting new laws.”

Wagle said 15 outdated Acts were repealed within half an hour of his assuming office as finance minister. He stressed that the government had also moved ahead with legal amendments that the private sector had been demanding for years.

He acknowledged that the economic reform process faced various challenges, saying it would take time to dismantle entrenched practices that had allowed the state to be exploited by capturing policies and institutions.

The government aims to achieve 7 percent economic growth over the coming decade and expand the size of Nepal’s economy to $100 billion, Wagle said.

“Government representatives have said that simply replicating past development models will not be possible if Nepal is to achieve sustained economic growth,” he said. “We need to focus on new economic opportunities in the 21st century.”

Infrastructure Minister Lamsal said the government was seeking to create a more favourable environment for development and investment by reforming existing laws.

Lamsal said legal measures would be taken to address problems affecting investment and development.

“The government is focused on drafting citizen-friendly laws,” he said. “An Act is the mirror of a country. The kind of laws we make determines the kind of nation we become.”

He said the workshop would play an important role in efforts to make infrastructure development more dynamic and effective and identify necessary reforms.

“If you look at the Urban Development Act, you can see the kind of cities we have; similarly, the kind of Education Act we have is reflected in our schools,” Lamsal said. “The results appear to depend on the laws we make.”

He said the government was seeking to improve laws that are currently being revised.

“We need to study the drafts we have prepared word by word and think about how to make the laws even better,” Lamsal said. “When we were passing the Public Procurement Act, the Federation of Contractors’ Associations of Nepal came up with a suggestion, but we did not adopt it because it did not amount to a policy departure.”

He said the government nevertheless studied the suggestions submitted by stakeholders.

Law Minister Gautam said the government had designated the current fiscal year as the “Year of Lawmaking and Reform” and set a target of registering 166 bills in Parliament.

Gautam said the government had accelerated the drafting and reform of laws in line with its policy priorities.

The lawmaking process involves the government preparing and registering government bills, while Parliament is responsible for passing them, she stressed.

Around 54 bills have already been approved by the Cabinet since the beginning of the current fiscal year. Those bills are in the process of being registered in Parliament, the minister said.

“The government has worked out clear policy positions on the future direction of development and reforms required by various ministries, the necessary legal reforms have been identified and work has been initiated accordingly,” Gautam said.

She said the rapid process of lawmaking and reform should focus on investment and development in the infrastructure sector.

“Financial resources alone are not sufficient for a country to achieve economic prosperity,” she said. “It also needs the right policies, capable institutions and effective structures.”

She said the workshop organised by the infrastructure ministry to discuss legal reforms with investment and development at the centre was a positive start to the broader law reform process.

The workshop, which runs until Sunday, is organised in partnership with the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, the Confederation of Nepalese Industries, the Nepal Chamber of Commerce and the Federation of Contractors’ Associations of Nepal. It is a part of preparations for the Nepal Infrastructure Conference 2026.

Nepal Chamber of Commerce President Kamlesh Kumar Agrawal said necessary legal and policy reforms were needed to prioritise infrastructure development, enhance competitiveness and support economic growth.

He stressed the need to make legal procedures for infrastructure development simpler, clearer and more transparent.

“At a time when the global economy is changing rapidly, modern and reliable infrastructure is indispensable for advancing investment, technology, production, trade, tourism, employment and economic activity,” he said.

Federation of Contractors’ Associations of Nepal President Nicholas Pandey said the infrastructure conference was directly linked to the country’s economic prosperity.

title: Tiny Boron Doses Supercharge Wheat Yields in Nepal’s Nitrogen-Hungry Fields - Bioengineer.org
description: Tiny Boron Doses Supercharge Wheat Yields in Nepal’s Nitrogen-Hungry Fields  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Wheat feeds more of humanity than almost any other crop, supplying roughly a fifth of the calories consumed by more than a third of the world’s population. Yet in Nepal, one of the countries that depends on it most heavily, average yields have stubbornly lagged behind those of neighboring South Asian producers. The 2024/25 marketing year placed national production at an estimated 2.1 million metric tons, with an average productivity of just 2.92 tonnes per hectare. For researchers trying to understand why, the answer increasingly points below the ground: to soils that are quietly starved of the nutrients wheat needs most, and to fertilizer guidelines that were never designed for the specific fields where farmers actually work.

A new field study conducted in Dhading, Nepal, and published in BMC Agriculture, offers some of the clearest evidence yet that the solution lies not in any single nutrient but in the interaction between two of them. Prabin Ghimire and Janma Jaya Gairhe, both of the Institute of Agriculture and Animal Science at Tribhuvan University, spent two consecutive growing seasons testing how nitrogen and boron, applied alone and in combination, shaped the yield, fertility, and soil chemistry of a wheat crop. Their central finding is striking: when the two nutrients were applied together at the right rates, grain yields climbed to levels far above the national average, and a persistent reproductive failure known as wheat sterility fell dramatically.

The problem the researchers set out to address is both agronomic and chemical. Nitrogen is the macronutrient that drives vegetative growth, tillering, and biomass accumulation in wheat, and decades of research have confirmed that raising nitrogen inputs generally raises grain yields. But the relationship is not linear. Excessive nitrogen can trigger diminishing returns, nutrient leaching, soil acidification, and lodging, the structural collapse of top-heavy plants. Boron, by contrast, is a micronutrient required in tiny amounts, but its role is outsized: it is essential for pollen viability and fertilization, and its deficiency is directly linked to spikelet sterility, the failure of flowers to set grain. In Nepal, boron-deficient soils are widespread and have long been associated with outbreaks of wheat sterility that slash harvests without any visible disease.

What has been missing, the authors argue, is field-scale evidence of how these two nutrients behave together, particularly in soils where both are deficient. Baseline analysis of the experimental site in Dhading, a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical location classified as a Dystric Loamic Fluvisol, revealed total nitrogen at just 0.14 percent and boron at 0.21 parts per million, both below the critical thresholds for optimal wheat growth. Government fertilizer recommendations in Nepal are typically issued for broad agroecological zones, with little allowance for site-specific soil chemistry, seasonal variability, or local climate. That gap leaves farmers applying nutrients in proportions that may be agronomically wrong for their fields, wasting money and degrading soil in the process.

To test the interaction directly, the team ran a split-plot experiment across the 2020 and 2021 cropping seasons using the medium-maturity wheat variety BL3063, obtained from Nepal’s National Wheat Research Program. Main plots received nitrogen at 0, 80, 100, or 120 kilograms per hectare, applied as urea in three splits: half incorporated before sowing, a quarter at 30 days after sowing, and a quarter at 60 days. Subplots received boron at 0, 1, or 2 kilograms per hectare as a basal dose. The design was replicated three times, and the researchers analyzed their results with linear mixed-effects models that treated year and replication as random effects, allowing them to separate genuine treatment effects from environmental noise. Grain yields were standardized to 14 percent moisture, and plant tissue nitrogen was measured by the micro-Kjeldahl method at three key phenological stages: tillering, booting, and grain filling.

The results were unambiguous. Nitrogen application significantly increased grain yield, biological yield, and straw yield, with the highest grain yield, 8,143.89 kilograms per hectare, recorded at 120 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare. That figure represents a 49.3 percent increase over the unfertilized control, which yielded 5,455.87 kilograms per hectare, and it dwarfs Nepal’s national average of roughly 2.99 tonnes per hectare. Tissue nitrogen concentrations rose consistently with application rate at every growth stage, peaking during tillering, which the authors interpret as confirmation of a clear dose-specific and phenological response. Boron, meanwhile, delivered its own kind of magic: applying it significantly reduced spikelet sterility and improved grain yield, with the effect visible in both seasons.

The most compelling numbers emerged from the interaction analysis. The lowest sterility rate, 33.2 percent, occurred under the combined treatment of 120 kilograms of nitrogen and 2 kilograms of boron per hectare, a 35.9 percent reduction compared with the control treatment, which suffered 51.8 percent sterility. Notably, the regression analysis revealed a consistent negative relationship between applied boron and sterility across both years, and the statistical groupings showed that even the moderate dose of 1 kilogram per hectare significantly outperformed the control. The authors attribute the synergy to boron’s role in nitrogen metabolism: the micronutrient facilitates nitrogen uptake, supports protein synthesis, and ensures effective pollen viability and fertilization, thereby maximizing grain set precisely when nitrogen availability is at its highest.

The soil story is more complicated, and it carries a warning. Post-harvest analysis of the top 20 centimeters of soil showed that increasing nitrogen rates significantly reduced soil pH, with the acidification effect more pronounced in 2021 than in 2020. This is consistent with the well-documented chemistry of nitrification, in which ammonium-based fertilizers release hydrogen ions as soil microbes convert ammonium to nitrate. Total soil nitrogen did increase with higher application rates, indicating a genuine fertility gain, and boron availability responded strongly to boron treatments, though with notable year-to-year variation likely driven by environmental factors. Phosphorus and potassium levels remained largely unchanged. The authors suggest that liming may be needed to counteract long-term acidification, and they emphasize that balanced fertilization, rather than nitrogen alone, is the key to maintaining soil health over time.

The study is not without limitations, and the authors are candid about them. Two growing seasons cannot capture the full arc of soil fertility dynamics or climate variability, and only one wheat variety was tested, leaving open the question of whether other genotypes would respond similarly. Sterility, moreover, can also be driven by temperature fluctuations and drought stress, for which site-specific data were not available. Still, the stability of the grain yield response across both years, and the absence of a significant three-way interaction between year, nitrogen, and boron, suggest that the underlying biology is robust. The practical implications are immediate: micronutrients like boron deserve a formal place in national fertilizer recommendations, not as an afterthought but as a co-equal partner to nitrogen. For a country striving toward wheat self-sufficiency, the path forward may run through a nutrient most farmers have never measured, applied at rates measured in single kilograms rather than hundreds, working quietly in the pollen tubes of every wheat flower to turn nitrogen into grain.

title: AI-generated video falsely linked to deadly landslides in Nepal - AFP Fact Check
description: AI-generated video falsely linked to deadly landslides in Nepal  AFP Fact Check
publisher.title: AFP Fact Check
full_article:
"Terrifying scenes of a landslide in the mountains of Nepal," reads an X post from September 29, 2026, in simplified Chinese.

It retweeted an Arabic-language post which includes a video showing a massive landslide cascading down a mountainside next to a white multi-storey building, sweeping away cars and trees in its path.

The clip was shared with similar claims across different social media platforms in multiple languages, including English, Hindi, Spanish and French.

Image Screenshot of the X post, taken on September 29, 2026, with a red X and an AI label added by AFP

Heavy rainfall triggered floods and landslides across northern India and neighbouring Nepal in late September 2026, leaving at least 68 people dead (archived link).

The Himalayan nation, where a devastating flood in late August killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands more missing, was hit by new flooding and landslides that killed at least 12 people.

Scientists have warned in recent years of an increase in extreme weather events across South Asia, linking them to rising temperatures and changing climate patterns.

But the video is AI-generated.

An analysis of the footage identified several visual anomalies that are hallmarks of AI-generated content.

The building's structure is blurred and distorted, and the flow of the debris making its way downhill is unnatural.

The powerful mudslide can be seen sweeping away cars and trees on the roads below, yet the figures on the left remain motionless without attempting to flee. Some poles along the side of the roads are seemingly unaffected by the massive landslide.

The video also shows debris falling at high speed from the very edge of a multi-storey building, yet the building remains unscathed.

High-rise constructions as seen in the video are not a common feature of Nepal's mountainous districts, where settlements are typically low-rise due to the steep terrain and limited flat land (archived here and here).

Image Screenshots of the false video, with visual inconsistencies highlighted and AI labels added by AFP

An analysis of the video using Hive Moderation, an AI detection tool, found it 99.4 percent "likely to contain AI-generated or deepfake content" (archived link).

Image Screenshot of the Hive Moderation analysis results, taken on September 29, 2026. AI symbol added by AFP

AFP has debunked other AI-generated misinformation.

KATHMANDU: Japanese encephalitis (JE) has been confirmed in 131 people across Nepal so far this year, with health authorities reporting 28 deaths from the infection.

According to the latest report from the Family Welfare Division under the Ministry of Health and Population, Nepal has recorded 1,372 cases of acute encephalitis syndrome in 2026, of which 131 have been confirmed as Japanese encephalitis.

The Division reported that 28 people have died from JE so far. It said 87 percent of those infected had not been vaccinated against the disease.

JE cases have been reported across 90 local levels in 37 districts. According to the report, most of those infected live near paddy fields or pig farms and are involved in agricultural activities.

The government is continuing its JE vaccination campaign in affected areas. The campaign is currently underway across all local levels of Jhapa district, as well as in Ghodaghodi Municipality, Dhangadhi Sub-Metropolitan City and Lamkichuha Municipality of Kailali district. The campaign is targeting people aged 30 and above, along with health workers. So far, 111,790 people in Kailali and 346,777 people in Jhapa have received the JE vaccine.

Under the routine immunization programme, the government provides a single dose of the JE vaccine to children at 12 months of age. Children who miss the scheduled dose can receive the vaccine up to the age of five.

Doctors have advised people to take precautions against mosquito bites in addition to getting vaccinated to reduce the risk of Japanese encephalitis.

title: Nepal’s artists raise money for flood survivors - nepalitimes.com
description: Nepal’s artists raise money for flood survivors  nepalitimes.com
publisher.title: nepalitimes.com
full_article:
When disaster strikes, artists often respond in the language they know best: through their work.

Journalists bring information in news photographs, videos, and reportage. Artists add an important emotional element to raise collective consciousness and spur action.

Nepal Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA) is organising a fundraising exhibition, Arts for Humanity, of paintings, photographs, and sculptures. Proceeds go to relief efforts for communities affected by last month’s Bhote Kosi-Trisuli flood.

Taking part in this unique initiative are Nepal’s established masters and emerging talent, with works by prominent artists including Thakur Prasad Mainali, Sharada Chitrakar, Mukti Simha Thapa, Vatsa Gopal Vaidya, alongside promising younger artists like Ishan Pariyar, Krishna Lama, Suman Thapa, Prakash Mijar, and others.

What makes the exhibition particularly remarkable is that the organisers at NAFA have put a price cap of Rs20,000 on every artwork on display. In many cases, art pieces whose market value would ordinarily run into hundreds of thousands of rupees will be available at a fraction of their usual price.

For collectors and first-time buyers alike, the exhibition presents a rare opportunity to acquire original works from some of Nepal’s most respected artists while contributing directly to a humanitarian cause.

“This is perhaps one of those rare moments when art collecting and social responsibility come together so meaningfully,” says NAFA’s Erina Tamrakar. “Buyers will be not only be taking home a piece of art, they will be helping families rebuild their lives.”

Under the exhibition’s fundraising model, 70% of the proceeds from each sale will go directly to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, 10% will go to NAFA artists’ welfare fund, and 20% is allocated to the participating artist. However, many artists have voluntarily chosen to donate their entire share, ensuring that 100% of the sale value of their work supports relief efforts and the artists’ welfare fund.

The initiative highlights the long-standing role of Nepal’s artistic community in responding to national crises. Beyond their aesthetic value, the works on display become expressions of solidarity with communities facing loss and uncertainty.

Visitors can see a diverse range of artistic styles and mediums, from contemporary paintings and documentary photography to sculpture and mixed-media works. They reflect both the richness of Nepal’s creative landscape and the willingness of artists to contribute beyond the studio.

Rebuilding will necessarily begin with practical necessities like shelter, food, and infrastructure. Yet the exhibition conveys the message that recovery depends on solidarity.

full_article:
Kate Adie introduces stories from Nepal, Gaza, Ukraine, the USA and Norway.

Recent catastrophic floods have heightened fears among Nepal's many at-risk mountain communities living under the looming threat of melting glaciers. Antonia Bolingbroke-Kent reports from the village and monastery of Halji in the country's high plains.

UNICEF says some 98 per cent of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, which began after the Hamas attacks of October 7 2023. In recent weeks, the Ministry of Education announced it was going ahead with the new academic year, leading to hundreds of thousands of children returning to the classroom for the first time in three years. Lina Shaikhouni has been speaking to one teenage girl about her experience.

This week Ukraine suffered the biggest attack on its energy infrastructure since the Spring. Relentless Russian drone strikes are now common across the capital and other major cities. BBC diplomatic correspondent Paul Adams reports from Kyiv on the changing nature of the war.

For decades, many in Florida’s Cuban-American community have dreamed of regime change on the Communist-run island, which many left as children. Will Grant met a group of Cuban-American entrepreneurs in Miami formulating plans for the future.

When Norway’s capital Oslo was in the process of transforming its waterfront from an industrial space to one for public recreation, city planners initially knocked back a maverick idea to launch floating saunas in the fjord. But a local footballer took a selfie next to the initial prototype – and the idea took off. Chelsea Coates has been to test it out.

title: British Gurkha veterans issue ultimatum to Nepal government over long-standing grievances - The Kathmandu Post
description: British Gurkha veterans issue ultimatum to Nepal government over long-standing grievances  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The British Gurkha Satyagraha United Struggle Committee has issued an ultimatum to the Nepal government, calling for progress on what it describes as long-standing grievances over the pay, pensions, recognition and treatment of British Gurkha veterans.

The committee is part of tripartite talks involving the governments of Nepal and the United Kingdom and Gurkha veterans campaigning for reforms.

In a letter addressed to Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Friday, the committee said it would resume peaceful protests, including hunger strikes and solidarity actions in Nepal and the UK, if its demands are not addressed by December 31, 2026.

Several rounds of talks have been held in London to address the veterans’ demands, but they have yet to produce a settlement. The UK and Nepal governments have been engaged in bilateral discussions for more than four years, following hunger strikes in 2021 by Gurkha veterans Gyanraj Rai, Dhan Gurung and Pushpa Rana Ghale.

A former Nepali ambassador to the UK said the British government had proposed the idea of a package settlement for Gurkha veterans who have long campaigned against disparities in pay and pensions. But no agreement has been reached between the veterans and the British government, the former ambassador said.

The veterans’ campaign has continued for decades. According to the committee, more than 20,000 Gurkha veterans have died since the campaign began, while elderly pensioners continue to die before their demands are resolved.

The veterans are seeking pension parity with British Army personnel and the implementation of provisions they say arise from the 1947 Tripartite Agreement, among other demands.

In 2009, with the support of British actress Joanna Lumley, Gurkhas who had retired before 1997 won the right to settle in the UK. Campaigners, however, continued to seek equal pensions and welfare benefits for veterans who retired before 1997.

The UK government rejected those demands, prompting former Gurkhas to stage hunger strikes in 2013 and 2021, lasting 15 and 13 days respectively. Following the protests, the British government agreed to hold talks, but campaigners say the process has been repeatedly delayed or disrupted by changes in the UK government.

The committee, led by chief coordinator Krishna Bahadur Rai, said its demands stem from what it regards as unequal treatment of Gurkhas who served in the British Army. It cited the 1923 Britain-Nepal Friendship Treaty and the 1947 Tripartite Agreement as key foundations for its claims.

According to the letter, Gurkha representatives have taken part in government-to-government discussions since 2017. A technical committee formed as part of the process produced a report in 2018 proposing reforms to address the veterans’ grievances. The committee says subsequent negotiations have failed to produce a comprehensive settlement.

It also referred to the 2021 hunger strike and other peaceful protests. According to the committee, an agreement reached in August that year provided for Gurkha grievances to be addressed through government-to-government talks, with the 2018 Technical Committee Report serving as a reference.

Among its main demands, the committee is seeking a fully costed and binding implementation schedule covering 11 financial issues that it says were identified in the 2018 report and incorporated into the 2021 framework.

It is also seeking a written response to correspondence from its independent adviser, retired Lieutenant Colonel Hamish Adams, on the constitutional and service identity of British Gurkhas.

The committee has called for the release of historical records relating to Gurkha recruitment and terms of service, citing the UK’s Public Records Act and arguing that greater transparency is needed.

Retrospective pension parity is another central issue. The committee argues that previous changes to Gurkha pension arrangements demonstrate that retrospective adjustments are possible. It also disputes the treatment of earlier periods of Gurkha service and says their service should be recognised on an equal basis.

The committee said the issue has become increasingly urgent because of the age of surviving veterans. It claimed that more than 20,000 affected veterans have died since campaigns over Gurkha grievances began.

The group also referred to Nepal’s 2022 decision to suspend the recruitment of Nepali citizens into the Indian Army following changes to India’s military recruitment system. It suggested that a review of UK recruitment arrangements could become necessary if its demands remain unresolved.

The committee’s letter calls for Gurkhas who joined the British Army between January 1, 1948, and September 30, 1993, to be treated equally and for the Tripartite Agreement to be honoured.

One of the 55 Malaysian nationals missing after the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods has finally been found after 37 days and has safely returned home, a group representing the individuals has announced.

The group, named Malaysia Solidarity: Families in Hope (Masfih), said on Friday that the missing person – a Chinese Malaysian solo traveller who had gone to Nepal – reported themselves to the Malaysian embassy in Kathmandu.

"For Masfih and the other families, the finding of a safe Malaysian 37 days later is an extremely relieving and meaningful development," Masfih spokesperson Manivannan Rethinam said in a statement.

(REUTERS)

The devastating floods, triggered by a Himalayan glacier collapse and avalanche near Langtang Lirung, claimed the lives of over 1,400 people, with more than 5,000 people still missing in Nepal, with hundreds unaccounted for in neighbouring Tibet and China.
